props.title: I Shot Andy Warhol

sections.content: I Shot Andy Warhol delivers a searing portrait of radical feminist Valerie Solanas through Lili Taylor's explosive performance. The film captures the feverish energy of Warhol's Factory scene while diving deep into Solanas's descent from brilliant writer to would-be assassin. Director Mary Harron expertly recreates 1960s counterculture New York, showing how Solanas's SCUM Manifesto emerged from genuine revolutionary fervor before paranoia and rejection pushed her to violence. The film pairs naturally with other artistic-scene biopics like Basquiat (1996) and Factory Girl (2006), but takes a darker, more politically charged approach.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in how it contextualizes Solanas within the broader feminist and artistic movements of the 1960s. Like Born in Flames (1983) and She's Beautiful When She's Angry (2014), it shows how radical politics emerged from genuine oppression. Harron's direction maintains remarkable objectivity - neither condemning nor glorifying Solanas while showing how mental illness and social rejection fueled her extremism. The Factory scenes with Jared Harris as Warhol capture both the scene's creative energy and its casual cruelty. SUBHEAD: The Factory on Film

Warhol's Factory has inspired numerous films, but few capture its dark underbelly like I Shot Andy Warhol. While Factory Girl (2006) focuses on the glamour and tragedy of Edie Sedgwick, and Chelsea Girls (1966) provides Warhol's own experimental view, Harron's film exposes the scene's exploitation and exclusion. The power dynamics between Warhol and his "superstars" become a microcosm of larger social hierarchies that Solanas raged against. Stephen Dorff's candy-colored performance as Candy Darling provides crucial perspective on the Factory's complex gender politics.
